column1: 429|Alcohols have –OH on an aliphatic carbon (ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH); phenols have –OH directly on an aromatic ring (phenol, C₆H₅OH); ethers have oxygen between carbon groups (diethyl ether, C₂H₅OC₂H₅).
430|Butan-2-ol.
431|In a primary alcohol the carbon bearing OH is attached to one other carbon; in a secondary alcohol to two; in a tertiary alcohol to three.
432|Alcohol molecules form intermolecular hydrogen bonds through –OH groups. More energy is needed to separate them than comparable alkanes, which rely mainly on dispersion forces.

433|Intermolecular hydrogen bonds raise alcohol boiling points. The –OH group hydrogen-bonds with water, making lower alcohols soluble; as the hydrophobic alkyl chain grows, water solubility decreases.
434|Hydrate ethene with steam over a phosphoric-acid catalyst at elevated temperature/pressure: CH₂=CH₂+H₂O⇌CH₃CH₂OH.
435|Heat a haloalkane with aqueous NaOH or KOH; OH⁻ substitutes for halide to give the alcohol, R–X+OH⁻→R–OH+X⁻.
436|Aldehydes reduce to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols, e.g. with NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ followed by work-up: RCHO→RCH₂OH; R₂CO→R₂CHOH.
437|A primary alcohol under controlled oxidation gives an aldehyde, RCH₂OH+[O]→RCHO+H₂O; distil promptly or use a mild reagent to limit further oxidation to the carboxylic acid.

438|Primary alcohols oxidise first to aldehydes and, under stronger/continued conditions, carboxylic acids. Secondary alcohols give ketones. Tertiary alcohols resist mild oxidation; strong conditions may cleave C–C bonds.
439|Lucas test uses concentrated HCl with anhydrous ZnCl₂ to convert alcohols to insoluble alkyl chlorides. Turbidity time distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols approximately.

440|Tertiary alcohols turn cloudy almost immediately, secondary alcohols after minutes, while primary alcohols show little/no turbidity at room temperature; carbocation stability controls the usual SN1-like rate order 3°>2°>1°.
441|Ethanol forms sodium ethoxide and hydrogen: 2C₂H₅OH+2Na→2C₂H₅ONa+H₂↑.
442|Dehydration removes H₂O from an alcohol, usually forming an alkene under acid/heat or an ether under suitable lower-temperature conditions.

443|First protonate ethanol’s OH to make H₂O a leaving group. Loss of water and removal of a β-H occur in an E2-like elimination for primary ethanol, forming CH₂=CH₂; acid is regenerated. No stable primary carbocation is required.
444|Concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates –OH so it can leave as water and, as a dehydrating agent, favours water removal; temperature helps control alkene versus ether formation.

445|Tertiary alcohols can form more stable carbocations after protonated water leaves, facilitating E1 dehydration; secondary are intermediate and primary are least favourable (often eliminate by a concerted route).
446|Diethyl ether (ethoxyethane), C₂H₅OC₂H₅, forms predominantly at about 413 K: 2C₂H₅OH→C₂H₅OC₂H₅+H₂O.
447|At about 413 K, intermolecular dehydration gives diethyl ether. At about 443 K with concentrated H₂SO₄, intramolecular elimination gives ethene, CH₂=CH₂.
448|Phenol is hydroxybenzene, with an –OH group directly attached to a benzene ring; formula C₆H₅OH (C₆H₆O).
449|Phenol loses H⁺ to form phenoxide, whose negative charge is delocalised into the aromatic ring. Ethoxide has no comparable resonance stabilisation, so ethanol is much less acidic.
450|Phenoxide’s negative charge is delocalised over oxygen and ortho/para ring positions by resonance. Ethoxide’s charge remains localised mainly on oxygen, so phenoxide is more stable.
451|An electron-withdrawing group stabilises phenoxide by inductive and/or resonance effects, especially at ortho/para positions, and increases phenol acidity.
452|Acidity: p-nitrophenol>phenol>p-cresol. The para nitro group withdraws and stabilises phenoxide; the methyl group donates electron density and destabilises it.
453|In the Dow process, chlorobenzene reacts with aqueous NaOH at high temperature and pressure to form sodium phenoxide; acidification gives phenol: C₆H₅Cl→C₆H₅ONa→C₆H₅OH.
454|Bromine water rapidly substitutes at the activated ortho and para positions to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate, decolourising bromine water.
455|The –OH group donates a lone pair into the aromatic ring by resonance, increasing ring electron density and stabilising ortho/para arenium-ion intermediates; phenol reacts faster than benzene.
456|Kolbe–Schmitt reaction: sodium phenoxide reacts with CO₂ under pressure/heat to form sodium salicylate; acidification yields salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid).
457|Reimer–Tiemann reaction formylates phenol mainly at the ortho position using CHCl₃ and aqueous NaOH, followed by acid work-up, to give salicylaldehyde.
458|Main product is 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde). CHCl₃/NaOH generates dichlorocarbene, :CCl₂, which introduces the formyl group after hydrolysis.
459|Dilute HNO₃ gives a mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol by electrophilic substitution; the para isomer is often major.
460|Dilute HNO₃ gives mainly ortho- and para-nitrophenol. Concentrated HNO₃ causes further nitration to 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid).
461|Add neutral FeCl₃: phenol gives a violet/purple coloured complex, whereas ethanol does not give this characteristic colour.
462|An ether has an oxygen atom bonded to two carbon groups: R–O–R′ (which may be identical or different).
463|Methoxyethane.
464|Williamson synthesis: react a sodium alkoxide/phenoxide with a suitable primary alkyl halide by SN2: RONa+R′X→ROR′+NaX.
465|A primary halide is least sterically hindered and undergoes SN2 substitution readily. Secondary/tertiary halides increasingly favour E2 elimination with the alkoxide base.

466|Propene is usually the major product by E2 elimination because 2-bromopropane is secondary and ethoxide is a strong base. A smaller amount of ethyl isopropyl ether may form by competing SN2 substitution.
467|Excess hot HI cleaves both C–O bonds of a dialkyl ether: C₂H₅OC₂H₅+2HI→2C₂H₅I+H₂O.

468|Protonate ether oxygen, then I⁻ usually attacks the less hindered alkyl group by SN2. If one side is tertiary, cleavage at that side can proceed by SN1; in aryl–alkyl ethers the alkyl–O bond breaks, giving phenol and alkyl iodide.

469|Alcohols can donate and accept intermolecular hydrogen bonds; ethers can accept but cannot donate O–H hydrogen bonds. Weaker intermolecular association gives ethers lower boiling points than isomeric alcohols.
470|Diethyl ether has been used as a solvent and historically as a general anaesthetic; its flammability and peroxide hazard require careful handling.
471|Oxygen and light can initiate radical autoxidation at α-C–H positions of ethers, forming explosive hydroperoxides/peroxides that may concentrate during storage or distillation.
472|Methanol is metabolised to formaldehyde and formate, causing metabolic acidosis, optic-nerve damage/blindness and potentially death; even small ingestions are medical emergencies.
473|Ethanol dissolves many polar and moderately non-polar substances, mixes with water, evaporates readily and is relatively accessible, making it useful in formulations, cleaning and extraction.

474|Methanol is made mainly from synthesis gas and used as a feedstock/solvent/fuel; it is highly toxic and can cause blindness or death. Ethanol is made by fermentation or ethene hydration and used as solvent/fuel; drinking it is intoxicating and excessive exposure is harmful.
475|Esterification is formation of an ester from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid, usually reversibly under acid catalysis: RCOOH+R′OH⇌RCOOR′+H₂O.
476|CH₃COOH+C₂H₅OH⇌CH₃COOC₂H₅+H₂O. Acid catalyses carbonyl activation and proton transfers; it accelerates attainment of equilibrium but does not change the equilibrium constant.
477|Water solubility generally decreases as the carbon chain length increases: the non-polar hydrophobic portion becomes larger relative to the hydrogen-bonding –OH group.
478|Phenol’s –OH can hydrogen-bond with water, but its large hydrophobic phenyl ring is poorly hydrated; this limits solubility compared with lower alcohols.

479|On oxidation, primary alcohols give aldehydes and then carboxylic acids; secondary alcohols give ketones; tertiary alcohols resist ordinary mild oxidation and require harsh conditions that may cleave C–C bonds.
480|2-Methylpropan-2-ol.
481|2-Methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, is the major alkene from acid-catalysed dehydration of 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

483|Electron-withdrawing −I groups stabilise phenoxide and increase acidity; at ortho/para positions, −M groups can further delocalise charge by resonance. Electron-donating +I/+M groups destabilise phenoxide and reduce acidity; effects depend on position.
484|Controlled bromination in a non-polar solvent (e.g. Br₂ in CS₂, low temperature) gives mainly p-bromophenol, with some o-bromophenol; conditions limit further substitution.

485|Bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol rapidly because phenoxide-like resonance strongly activates all ortho/para positions. In a non-polar solvent under controlled conditions, monobromination occurs, with para usually favoured over ortho.

488|A phenol oxygen lone pair is conjugated with the aromatic π system, giving the aryl C–O bond partial double-bond character; this makes it shorter than a typical alcohol C–O single bond.

492|Acid protonates/activates the carbonyl and facilitates nucleophilic addition and proton transfers, speeding esterification. It is regenerated and does not alter the equilibrium position.
